An agentic AI system for automated
pharmacogenomic recommendation
generation
Check for updates
Mike Zack
, Anton Savinkov, Danil Stupichev, Alex Moore, David Sokolov, Igor Trifonov,
Anastasia Yankovskiy, Kirill Reshetnikov, Nurkyz Ydyrysova & Allan Gobbs
Pharmacogenomic guidelines are essential for tailoring drug therapy to individual genetic proﬁles, but
current curation workﬂows are manual, resource‑intensive, time‑bound, and limited in coverage. We
introduce an agentic AI system for automated, scalable generation of CPIC-style recommendations
using large language models (LLMs) guided by structured evidence. Our modular pipeline retrieves
and processes full-text biomedical literature and FDA drug labels, extracts clinically relevant entities
with high accuracy (91.9% across 22 articles), aggregates ﬁndings across studies, and generates
phenotype-speciﬁc dosing recommendations for gene–drug pairs. In expert evaluations of 24 random
recommendations, our system signiﬁcantly outperformed leading LLM baselines (GPT-5, Claude,
Grok) in clinical clarity and guideline concordance. These results demonstrate the feasibility of using
evidence-grounded, agentic AI for end-to-end pharmacogenomic evidence synthesis, offering a path
toward broader population coverage, faster updates, and more consistent and explainable decision
support.
Pharmacogenomics (PGx) aims to tailor drug therapy based on individual
genetic variation, improving both efﬁcacy and safety. To support clinical
adoption, expert consortia such as CPIC1 (Clinical Pharmacogenetics
Implementation Consortium, now part of ClinPGx) and DPWG have
developed evidence-based guidelines that map genetic variants to dosing
adjustments or drug selection rules. These guidelines are widely used in
translational research and precision medicine but suffer from two major
limitations1: the high cost and slow pace of manual curation, and2 limited
coverage of gene–drug pairs and population contexts. As a result, many
actionable variants remain unaddressed, and important guideline updates
are often delayed by years.
Inthiswork,wefocusnotonpatient-leveltreatmentrecommendations
but on the automation of guideline-level evidence synthesis, generating
structured drafts that can support expert panels, hospital systems, and
clinical laboratories in updating and maintaining pharmacogenomic gui-
dance at scale.
A major bottleneck is that current workﬂows rely on extensive expert
involvement for every stage of guideline creation from identifying relevant
literature to extracting evidence and formulating recommendations. Even
large curated databases such as PharmGKB (now part of ClinPGx) fall short
of full coverage: their annotations are manually created and primarily
designed for human readability rather than machine interpretation. As a
result, integration into automated reasoning pipelines remains challenging,
and updates may lag behind the primary literature2. Prior efforts such as
PGxMine attempted to automate annotation pipelines for PharmGKB, but
these remained focused on entity-level extraction without translation into
dosing guidance3.
At the same time, large language models (LLMs) have shown
increasing promise in biomedical applications, including question
answering, summarization, and knowledge extraction. Recent studies have
explored the use of LLMs to support or even generate pharmacogenomic
recommendations by leveraging structured knowledge bases4,5 or free-text
literature6. In parallel, tools such as PubTator37 have improved normal-
ization of biomedical entities, enabling more reliable downstream reasoning
across heterogeneous corpora. These approaches suggest that LLMs, when
properly guided and grounded in context, may be capable of capturing
complex gene–drug–phenotype relationships, identifying dosing implica-
tions, and mimicking the structure and tone of CPIC-like guidelines.
Recent advances in artiﬁcial intelligence have introduced a new class of
systems known as “agentic AI”—models that go beyond passive informa-
tion retrieval to actively perceive, reason, and act within dynamic clinical
contexts8,9. Similar frameworks have also been applied in drug development
and due diligence, for example, LLM-based agent systems for competitive
landscape mapping of drug assets10, underscoring the broader utility of
agentic workﬂows in biomedicine. These agentic systems operate through a
perceive–reason–act loop, enabling them to analyze unstructured data,

formulate task plans, and autonomously execute actions such as generating
clinical summaries or initiating decision support8. In healthcare settings,
agentic AI has been shown to reduce administrative burdens, enhance
diagnostic workﬂows, and dynamically adapt to changing clinical states—
reducing hospital readmissions and improving triage accuracy9.
Agentic frameworks are also gaining traction in quantitative clinical
pharmacology and translational sciences, where autonomous agents
orchestrate multi-step tasks including PK/PD modeling, study simulation,
and regulatory document generation11. This multi-agent paradigm, often
described as “agentic workﬂows,” enables distributed automation across
drug development pipelines, providing both scalability and traceability. In
this context, pharmacogenomics stands out as a natural candidate for
agentic automation, due to the repetitive, evidence-driven nature of
guideline development. By deploying structured agentic reasoning, it
becomes possible to automatically identify gene–drug relationships, assess
supporting literature, and draft CPIC-style recommendations that are
explainable, reproducible, and continuously updatable while also main-
taining identiﬁable distinction from manually curated recommendations.
Our initial attempts followed a traditional path: training supervised
models to extract structured annotations from literature, mimicking the
format of PharmGKB. However, we found that this approach faced serious
challenges: inconsistent formatting in PDFs, limited data coverage, nor-
malization issues for genetic variants, and the high cost of gold-standard
labels. Importantly, even if perfect entity extraction were achieved, trans-
lating raw evidence into coherent, guideline-style recommendations
remained a non-trivial task.
Our system is designed to complement existing expert consortia such
as CPIC and DPWG, not replace them. By accelerating evidence synthesis
and providing transparent, traceable drafts, it aims to support expert
reviewers and enable faster, reproducible updates to clinical guidelines.
We therefore propose a generation-ﬁrst approach, in which LLMs are
used directly to synthesize guideline-like recommendations from raw bio-
medical literature. Instead of replicating existing curation schemas, we build
a hybrid pipeline that retrieves relevant documents, identiﬁes supporting
evidence using semantic search, and prompts an LLM to generate CPIC-
style recommendations, including dosage adjustments and rationale. This
system can operate both in de novo mode—proposing guidelines for pre-
viously uncurated gene–drug pairs—and in updater mode, suggesting
revisions for outdated guidelines, for example when new variants are
identiﬁed in an underrepresented population.
Inthispaper,wedescribethearchitectureandevaluationofoursystem.
We benchmark our method using expert-validated recommendations,
compare several prompting and retrieval strategies, and analyze limitations.
Wealsopositionourworkwithinrecenteffortstobenchmarkand specialize
LLMs for pharmacogenomics6,12 and discuss its implications for scalable
guideline development in precision medicine.
Results
System overview
To enable automated generation of pharmacogenomic recommendations,
we developed a modular system that processes literature and drug label
evidence
into
structured,
guideline-style
outputs.
The
PGxAI-
Recommender architecture comprises three stages: acquisition of relevant
texts, LLM-based extraction of evidence, and recommendation generation
based on structured input (Fig. 1, Supplementary Fig. 1).
This design reﬂects the culmination of iterative experimentation with
multiple prompting strategies, knowledge injection methods, and evalua-
tion setups. Early trials showed that even state-of-the-art LLMs, when
promptedsolelywithagene–drugpair,frequentlyreturnedvagueorgeneric
outputs, often omitting critical dosing adjustments. Simply adding all
relevant publications to a single prompt is not feasible, as the complete body
of evidence for a givengene–drug pair exceeds the available context window
of current LLMs. Moreover, an LLM with internet or web-search access
cannot reproduce the systematic, curated evidence aggregation performed
by guideline authors: ad hoc retrieval returns a limited and opportunistic
subset of publications rather than a comprehensive and structured synth-
esis. These limitations motivated a more structured, evidence-aware pipe-
line tailored to the complexities of pharmacogenomic decision-making.
Evaluation of extraction accuracy
We manually validated the outputs of the LLM-based evidence extraction
module on 22 pharmacogenomic articles. Three independent human
annotators evaluated the correctness of the extracted answers across 35
predeﬁned binary ﬁelds per article. In total, 2310 binary judgments were
collected across annotators and articles.
The model achieved an overall accuracy of 91.9%, deﬁned as the
proportion of ﬁelds marked as correct by the annotators. Errors primarily
reﬂected incorrect or imprecise extractions, including occasional over-
speciﬁcation.

Evaluation of recommendation accuracy
To assess the clinical quality of generated pharmacogenomic recommen-
dations, we conducted a blinded expert review of outputs from ﬁve models.
Each recommendation was rated on a 0–10 scale based on alignment with
known CPIC guidelines, clinical clarity, and dosing appropriateness.
PGxAI-Recommender achieved the highest average expert score (mean
9.0), compared to baseline models with mean scores ranging from 6.2 to 7.8,
and outperformed all baseline LLMs in pairwise statistical comparisons
(p < 0.01; Fig. 3B).
To further contextualize the score-based evaluation, we conducted a
pairwise guideline-conformance assessment against CPIC reference
recommendations. In this analysis, we derived a relative ranking of models
based on expert preferences. PGxAI-Recommender achieved the highest
observed pairwise win rate (0.83), whereas baseline LLMs exhibited lower
win rates ranging from 0.17 to 0.78, indicating stronger alignment of
PGxAI-RecommenderoutputswithCPICguidance(SupplementaryFig.2).
A notable observation from the baseline comparison was that GPT-5,
despite being a more advanced model, did not improve recommendation
quality and in several cases produced less guideline-concordant outputs.
GPT-5occasionallygenerateddetaileddosinginstructionsthatcontradicted
CPIC guidance. In scenarios where all other models correctly returned “No
recommendation,” GPT-5 produced full therapeutic regimens with speciﬁc
milligram dosing and administration schedules, even though such infor-
mationwasneitherpresentin theevidencecorpusnorrequested bythetask.
In other instances, GPT-5 returned overly narrow dose values (for example,
a single ﬁxed efavirenz dose) where CPIC requires expressing a dose range.
These deviations represent over-generation rather than guideline-aligned
reasoning and likely contributed to its lower expert scores relative to earlier
GPT models.
Three representative cases highlight the model’s strengths.
Efavirenz – CYP2B6 (Multiple Phenotypes)
CPIC provides nuanced, phenotype-speciﬁc guidance for efavirenz,
recommendingdosereductionsforintermediateandpoormetabolizersand
careful monitoring or escalation for ultrarapid metabolizers. The PGxAI-
Recommender consistently produced accurate and differentiated outputs
across all phenotypes. For intermediate and poor metabolizers, it suggested

900 mg), diverging from established recommendations. This case illustrates
the system’s ability to align with guideline logic even in edge phenotypes

Fluorouracil – DPYD (normal and poor metabolizers)
For normal metabolizers, CPIC advises standard dosing without mod-
iﬁcation. Most baseline models, however, added unnecessary regimen
details (e.g., “400–600 mg/m²/day” or complex bolus + infusion schedules),
which could mislead clinicians and complicate justiﬁcation during adverse
events. In contrast, the PGxAI-Recommender returned the concise and
guideline-aligned statement, standard dosing with no changes, avoiding
extraneous detail. For poor metabolizers, CPIC guidance is clear: avoid
ﬂuorouracil or related prodrugs due to the risk of severe, potentially life-
threatening toxicity. If no alternatives exist, only a highly reduced dose with
intensive therapeutic drug monitoring may be considered. The PGxAI-
Recommender precisely captured this “no safe use” stance, stating that
ﬂuorouracil should be avoided and offering no ambiguous fallback. Other
models tended to hedge, some suggested 25–50% of the standard dose or
addedvagueregimen-speciﬁccaveats,whichcouldexposepatientstoundue
risk. Our system’s categorical rejection aligns most closely with clinical best
practice, reducing the chance of misinterpretation in critical care settings.
Atorvastatin – SLCO1B1 (poor function)
CPIC suggests avoiding high-dose atorvastatin and considering alternatives
such as pravastatin. The PGxAI-Recommender explicitly recommended
≤20 mg/day or switching to a safer statin, whereas other models proposed
standard dose ranges (e.g., 10–80 mg/day) or omitted alternatives alto-
gether. Our system framed dose reduction in the context of broader ther-
apeutic strategy, yielding a more actionable and complete recommendation.
These ﬁndings highlight the value of evidence-aware prompting and
structured input design in generating high-quality, guideline-concordant
pharmacogenomic recommendations.
Discussion
Our evaluation demonstrates that LLMs can reliably extract structured
evidence when provided with curated, task-speciﬁc context. The extraction
module achieved an overall ﬁeld-level correctness rate of 91.9% across 22
pharmacogenomic studies, as assessed by independent expert annotators.
Agreement with the majority expert consensus was 94.7%, indicating that
the majority of extracted ﬁelds were judged acceptable by domain experts.
At the same time, inter-rater reliability metrics (Cohen’s and Fleiss’ κ)
revealed variability among expert judgments. This variability reﬂects both
the imbalancebetween correct and incorrect labels and differencesin expert
interpretation for a subset of ﬁelds, rather than systematic extraction errors.
Together,theseresultsindicatethatwhileexpertconsensusprovidesauseful
operational reference, some degree of disagreement is intrinsic to the task
and should be taken into account when interpreting extraction
performance.

A key difference between the PGxAI-Recommender and baseline
models such as GPT-4.1 lies in how each system uses evidence. GPT-4.1
reliessolely on a single prompt applied toan isolated gene–drug–phenotype
description, without access to aggregated multi-study evidenceorFDA label
information. In contrast, our system integrates structured inputs assembled
across several upstream stages, including study-level annotations, multi-
document evidence summaries, FDA excerpts, and a qualitative evidence
level. This consolidated evidence block provides explicit grounding signals,
numeric results, consistency across studies, phenotype deﬁnitions, and
regulatory context, that the generator is required to use when formulating
the ﬁnal recommendation. This architecture reduces unsupported asser-
tions, improves dose-range ﬁdelity, and enables the system to capture
guideline-speciﬁc subtleties (such as recommending alternative agents or
monitoring strategies) that GPT-4.1 frequently omitted or expressed
incompletely. We believe this deeper evidence integration explains the
observed performance gap in expert ratings.
Importantly, the observed performance gains reﬂect the use of struc-
tured,guideline-relevant context and prompt designrather thananychange
to the underlying language models. PGxAI-Recommender does not involve
model training or ﬁne-tuning. All models were evaluated in an inference-
only setting without internet access.
Together, these ﬁndings highlight the utility of evidence-aware
prompting for achieving guideline-concordant outputs, and support the
use of structured knowledge to enhance reliability in clinical NLP
applications.
Beyond accuracy, our system demonstrates the potential for broader
coverage and more up-to-date evidence compared to existing expert-
curated resources. As summarized in Table 1, the CPIC corpus currently
includes 316 gene–drug pairs and roughly 8000 cited articles, reﬂecting
guidelines published between 2014 and 2025. In contrast, the proposed
automated framework can identify up to 573 gene–drug pairs and retrieve
nearly 20,000 relevant pharmacogenomic publications indexed in PubMed
(1966–2025),supportingthegenerationofcontinuouslyupdated,literature-
grounded recommendations that align with the evolving evidence base.
Although the extraction and recommendation evaluations relied on a
relatively small set of manually reviewed articles22 and recommendations,24
these analyses were intended as a feasibility assessment rather than a full
validation study. The system itself is built to operate at much larger scale,
and future work will include validation on substantially expanded and more
heterogeneous evaluation sets as additional expert-curated data become
available.
Access to full-text articles represents an additional practical limitation.
Many pharmacogenomic studies are distributed across heterogeneous
publisher platformswith inconsistentopen-access availability.Tomaximize
coverage, the retrieval module attempts multiple pathways, including PMC,
DOI-redirected publisher pages, and applies PDF parsing and OCR-based
extraction when needed. Nevertheless, studies available only behind pay-
walls remain inaccessible to the current pipeline, which may introduce
coverage gaps or bias toward open-access literature. Future iterations could
incorporate licensed full-text sources or publisher partnerships where
permitted.
Although several domain-speciﬁc ﬁne-tuned models exist, including
BioMedLM16, BioGPT17, and Me-LLaMA18 variants trained on PubMed or
clinical corpora, we did not include them in the present evaluation for two
main reasons. First, in the context of multi-step evidence synthesis—which
requires long-context handling, and reliable adherence to structured
prompts—recent general-purpose LLMs substantially outperform domain-
speciﬁc models. Second, preliminary exploratory tests (conducted outside
the scope of this manuscript) indicated that while domain-adapted models
performed adequately on narrow extraction tasks, they were markedly less
reliable in tasks requiring multi-document integration and structured
recommendation generation. Given these limitations, and considering the
rapid progression of frontier LLM capabilities, we focused the formal eva-
luation on state-of-the-art general-purpose models.Future work mayrevisit
domain-speciﬁcarchitecturesastheycontinuetomatureandaslarger,more
comprehensive biomedical training corpora become available.
Panel-based guideline development remains the gold standard, and
our system is intended to support, not replace, expert-driven curation by
accelerating evidence synthesis and producing traceable drafts for review.
Several community initiatives already contribute to systematizing phar-
macogenomic knowledge at scale, including automated extraction pipelines
and expert-curated resources. PGxMine, for example, leverages large-scale
text mining across PubMed to surface gene–drug–variant signals, offering
broad coverage but necessarily limited to shallow associations rather than
full study-level evidence. Complementary resources such as PharmGKB
and its successor ClinPGx remain authoritative repositories built through
expert review, standardized annotation, and consensus-based evidence
grading. The framework described here is designed to operate alongside
these efforts: it uses a multi-step, evidence-synthesis workﬂow to integrate
ﬁndings across studies and generate guideline-formatted drafts, providing a
bridge between automated discovery pipelines and expert curation while
remaining aligned with established community standards.
While this study focuses on gene–drug pairs, real-world pharmaco-
genomic decision‑making also depends on broader context, including
drug–drug interactions, phenoconversion, prior treatments, polygenic
inﬂuences, patient age, comorbidities, and disease-speciﬁc factors. The
current system does not model these factors directly, but its modular evi-
dence schema is compatible with incorporating additional structured
inputs. Extending the pipeline to capture these modiﬁers represents an
important direction for future work.
Beyond these clinical modiﬁers, the capabilities of the described
approach are not limited to CPIC-style gene–drug recommendations. The
modular structure and agentic controller can be adapted to alternative
pharmacogenomic standards, including DPWG or others. It can also be
extended beyond pharmacogenomic guidelines. In principle, the same
architecture can incorporate additional molecular modalities, such as
transcriptomic activity, metabolomic signatures, or other omics-derived
features, whenever sufﬁcient evidence data are available. Extending the
system to these broader contexts represents an important direction for
future development.
The currentreportrepresentsa preliminaryestimate rather thana fully
validated corpus, however, it illustrates the scalability of our automated
pipeline and its capacity to incorporate emerging evidence from the latest
literature in conjunction with expert review. This expanded scope supports
applications beyond traditional curation, including faster updates, context-
speciﬁc recommendations, and broader population coverage.
Methods
End-to-end system for pharmacogenomic recommendation
generation
This section describes the full architecture and operational ﬂow of the
PGxAI-Recommender system as designed for real-world deployment,
capable of retrieving, processing, and integrating new evidence con-
tinuously. The process is composed of several steps described below.

Drug–gene pair selection
The process begins by carefully selecting a speciﬁc drug and gene pair of
interest. This selection is crucial because it deﬁnes the scope of the literature
review and data sources that will be queried in the subsequent steps.
Understanding the interaction between a particular drug and genetic var-
iations is a fundamental aspect of precision medicine.
These studies are highly important as they provide insights into how
genetic differences among individuals can inﬂuence the efﬁcacy and safety
of medications. For clinicians, having detailed knowledge about multiplex
drug–gene interactions enables more informed decision-making when
prescribing treatments. This helps to optimize therapeutic outcomes,
minimize adverse drug reactions, and tailor treatments to the genetic proﬁle
of each patient.
Ultimately, investigating drug–gene pairs supports the development of
precisionmedicinestrategies,allowinghealthcareproviderstomovebeyond
the traditional “one-size-ﬁts-all” approach and towards more personalized,
effective, and safer therapies.
Literature retrieval
The system searches PubMed database (1966–2025) through the Entrez
Programming Utilities13. Structured queries are constructed using the fol-
lowing keywords: gene name AND drug name, searched across Title/
Abstract, MeSH Terms, and All Fields.
The search was designed to identify peer-reviewed articles, clinical
studies, and reviews describing gene–drug associations, pharmacokinetic or
pharmacodynamic effects, and genotype-guided dosing outcomes. For each
retrieved PMID, an attempt is made to download the article in XML format
from PubMed Central (PMC).
If the XML is successfully retrieved, the system parses and extracts
relevant textual content, carefully removing non-informative XML tags to
focus on the essential scientiﬁc information.
For PMIDs where XML-format articles are not available via PubMed,
retrieving full-text content poses a signiﬁcant challenge due to inconsistent
accessacross publishersand repositories.To addressthis, weimplemented a
robust retrieval module that systematically searches for full-text PDF ver-
sions across a variety of open-access sources, including publisher websites,
institutional repositories, and document aggregators: PMC, DOI redirect,
Springer, Wiley Online Library, Frontiers. If a PDF is successfully located, it
is processed using a dedicated parsing engine based on the pypdf Python
library to extract embedded text.
In cases where the PDF contains scanned images or non-extractable
text, the system applies an OCR fallback pipeline using pdf2image to render
the pages as images and pytesseract to extract text content. All extracted
texts, whether from XML, abstract, PDF, or OCR sources, are normalized,
cleaned, and stored in a centralized database indexed by PMID to ensure
traceability and reproducibility during downstream analysis.
Annotation via large language model (LLM)
To support the automation of clinical interpretation, each retrieved full-text
document is processed by a large language model (LLM) using a custom-
designed prompt tailored for pharmacogenomics. This step uses GPT-4.1
(OpenAI API, temperature = 1e-5), the most current model available at the
time of system development. The primary objective is to identify and extract
clinically relevant entities and relationships that would typically be assessed
manually by a domain expert.
The LLM identiﬁes key elements such as:
• Drug name
• Gene and speciﬁc allele(s)
• Pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) parameters
• Phenotypic consequences (e.g., metabolizer status)
• Comparative analysis of allelic variants
• Study-level associations and outcomes
This step enables the systematic extraction of high-value information
from unstructured texts, regardless of document format or writing style.
Example in Supplementary Table 1. The resulting structured annotations
are storedin the database and serve as the foundation for generating precise,
guideline-ready therapeutic recommendations.
Evaluation results and performance metrics are presented in a later
section of this paper.
Evidence aggregation across multiple studies
To improve consistency and reliability of downstream recommendations,
we implemented an intermediate step that aggregates structured ﬁndings
across multiple studies for each gene–drug pair. For every set of extracted
annotations (grouped by PubMed ID), the system clusters evidenceby allele
(e.g., *2, *4, rsIDs) and organizes results into clinical categories: enzyme
activity, dose adjustment, efﬁcacy, toxicity, and PK/PD outcomes. A lan-
guage model then summarizes the ﬁndings into uniﬁed evidence records,
modeled after CPIC-style evidence tables. These include:
• A brief description of the main effect (e.g., “reduced activity in carriers
of *2 A”)
• Supporting vs. conﬂicting references by PMID
• Type of evidence (e.g., Clinical, In vitro)
• Heuristic level of evidence (High/Moderate/Weak)
For each aggregated gene–drug–phenotype evidence block, the system
assigns a qualitative level of evidence (High, Moderate, or Weak) using an
LLM-driven assessment. Rather than imposing ﬁxed numerical thresholds,
we follow the principles articulated in the foundational CPIC evidence
framework14, which emphasize reproducibility, study quality, and con-
sistency across independent investigations.
The LLM receives a consolidated structured summary of all extracted
studies and applies the following criteria:
• High: consistent results from multiple well-designed studies, including
reproducible associations, clear directionality of effect, appropriate
statistical support, and concordant clinical or pharmacokinetic
outcomes.
• Moderate: ﬁndings supported by multiple studies but with limitations
such as smallersample sizes, partially inconsistent results, indirectness,
ormethodologicalconstraintsthatreduceconﬁdencebutstillindicatea
likely effect.
• Weak: insufﬁcient basis for determining a reliable effect because evi-
dence is sparse, contradictory, underpowered, methodologically lim-
ited, or lacks key components in the chain of inference.
These criteria are encoded directly in the LLM prompt, ensuring
consistent reasoning across cases and avoiding rigid numerical cutoffs that
may not generalize across heterogeneous study designs. While the process is
heuristic and LLM-mediated, it follows established qualitative frameworks
used in pharmacogenomic guideline development and provides a trans-
parent basis for downstream recommendation generation. An example
output from this step is provided in Supplementary Table 2.
Preparation of additional data
To incorporate regulatory guidance, the system retrieves FDA15 drug label
PDFs directly from the ofﬁcial Drugs@FDA database and the FDA Label
Search (NCTR) portal (U.S. Food and Drug Administration, accessed June
2025).ExtractedlabeltextisprocessedwithGPT-4.1usingacustomprompt
to extract key prescribing information, including dosage, pharmacogenetic
considerations, contraindications, and relevant warnings. The structured
output is stored in the database and used alongside literature-derived evi-
dence during recommendation generation. An example output from this
step is provided in Supplementary Table 3.

Recommendation generation
To generate structured clinical guidance, the system uses a dedicated
recommendation module built on GPT-4.1 via the OpenAI API (tem-
perature = 1e-5) with a task-speciﬁc prompt.
The model receives the following inputs:
• Aggregated evidence block: consolidated ﬁndings from multiple stu-
dies (Section 4.1), grouped by allele and outcome type (e.g., activity,
dose, efﬁcacy, toxicity, PK/PD).
• FDA drug label excerpts, including dosage and pharmacogenomic
considerations.
• Target gene–drug–phenotype triple for which a recommendation is
being generated.
The model is explicitly instructed to:
• Decide whether to use the drug for the speciﬁed phenotype.
• Suggest a dose (standard, reduced, increased) with numeric values
when possible.
• Specify administration frequency (e.g., once daily).
• Assign a recommendation strength: Strong, Moderate, or No
recommendation.
• The output follows a strict JSON format and serves as a guideline-style
recommendation compatible with CPIC structure.
This step is fully automated, consistent, and scalable—enabling the
generation of hundreds of phenotype-speciﬁc recommendations with
clinical clarity and traceable evidence provenance.
An example of the ﬁnal structured output is provided in Supplemen-
tary Table 4, with the corresponding JSON representation shown in Sup-
plementary Note 1.
Storing and continuous updates based on new publications
All structured annotations, aggregated evidence tables, and generated
recommendations are stored in a centralized database, indexed by PMID
andgene–drug–phenotypetriplet,enablingtraceability,reproducibility,and
scalable querying.
To ensure that recommendations remain up-to-date, the system per-
forms an automated weekly literature scan and incrementally re‑processes
affected gene–drug pairs. When new data is detected, the same processing
pipeline (retrieval →extraction →annotation →structuring →recom-
mendation) is re-run. This automated updating mechanism enables the
system to continuously maintain current and comprehensive pharmaco-
genomic knowledge. As a result, it supports generating high-quality,
evidence-based conclusions and recommendations that reﬂect the latest
scientiﬁc ﬁndings, thereby enhancing clinical decision-making and guide-
line accuracy over time.
Agentic orchestration
To coordinate the multi-step processing required for each gene–drug pair,
the PGxAI-Recommenderincorporatesa lightweightagenticcontrollerthat
operates using a perceive–reason–act loop. Instead of executing a ﬁxed
sequence of steps, the system exposes each processing module—literature
retrieval, document annotation, FDA label parsing, evidence aggregation,
and recommendation generation—as an independent callable tool. The
controller maintains a persistent state for every case in a dedicated results
table,withﬁeldsindicatingwhethereachstage(extract,annotate,fda,recs)is
pending, completed, or requires re-execution.
At runtime, the controller receives a high-level goal (e.g., “complete
processing for case X”) and periodically queries the database to perceive the
current state of that case. Based on this state, it reasons about which action is
required next: retrieving missing full texts, annotating newly downloaded
documents, aggregating available evidence into phenotype-speciﬁc Level-
of-Evidence summaries, or triggering guideline-style recommendation
generation. After each tool invocation, the controller writes updated results
and logs back to the database, forming a feedback loop in which subsequent
decisions depend entirely on the evolving system state rather than a pre-
determined pipeline.
This design enables the agent to skip already completed stages, repeat
failed or incomplete steps, adapt to heterogeneous document availability,
and terminate automatically once all required components have been
produced. The architecture therefore, supports robust error recovery,
deterministic state tracking, and transparent auditability while preserving
ﬂexibility in execution order. A concise version of the controller’s instruc-
tion prompt is provided in Supplementary Note 2, and a pseudocode
representation of the perceive–reason–act workﬂow is provided in Sup-
plementary Note 3. A schematic overview of the orchestration process is
included in Supplementary Fig. 1.
Experimental setup for evaluation
While the PGxAI-Recommender is designed for continuous evidence
integration from literature and regulatory sources (see “End-to-End System
for Pharmacogenomic Recommendation Generation”), the evaluation in
this paper was conducted on a ﬁxed set of 17 gene–drug pairs derived from
existing CPIC guidelines. Literature used for recommendation generation
was selected from the CPIC bibliography to enable direct comparison with
reference recommendations. The evaluation of the system was conducted in
two distinct stages to ensure both the accuracy of extracted annotations and
the clinical relevance of generated guideline recommendations.
Annotation validation
The ﬁrst evaluation stage assessed whether the LLM-based annotation
module accurately extracted clinically relevant information from primary
literature. Three human annotators, including a PGx-trained reviewer,
independently evaluated each extracted value and labeled it as correct or
incorrect for a random sample of 22 full-text articles. For each article,
annotators compared the structured outputs generated by the system with
the original text to assess whether key data points, such as gene variants,
phenotypic effects, and pharmacokinetic outcomes, were correctly identi-
ﬁed and extracted. Importantly, the extraction task requires the model to
produce a value for every predeﬁned ﬁeld in each article, and annotators
assessonlythecorrectnessofthegenerated value ratherthanthepresenceor
absence of the ﬁeld in the source text. The extracted ﬁelds span hetero-
geneous data types, including quantitative values, categorical descriptors,
and identiﬁers. As a result, classical positive and negative categories are not
uniformly applicable across ﬁelds in this evaluation. Accordingly, the eva-
luationfocusedoncompletenessandfactualaccuracyoftheannotationsasa
prerequisite for reliable downstream recommendation generation. Accu-
racy was calculated as the proportion of extracted ﬁelds that annotators
judged to be correct. Full expert scoring results are available on Zenodo
(DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.17727992).
Recommendation quality assessment
To evaluate clinical quality, we conducted a blinded expert review across a
representative subset of random 24 recommendations. Selection criteria
prioritized diversity across genes, drugs, and metabolizer phenotypes (e.g.,
poor, intermediate, ultrarapid), ensuring clinically meaningful variation.
To benchmark overall quality, we compared recommendations pro-
duced by the full PGxAI-Recommender—which integrates structured evi-
dence, regulatory label data, and gene–drug–phenotype logic—against
outputs from baseline large language models (GPT-4.1, GPT-4o-mini,
GPT-5, GPT-o3 by OpenAI; Claude Opus 4 by Anthropic; and Grok 4 by
xAI) prompted under identical conditions but without access to structured
evidence or curation logic. The exact prompt templates used for both the
baseline condition and the evidence-augmented recommendation module
are provided in Supplementary Notes 4 and 5. For clarity, the PGxAI-
Recommender and the “baseline GPT-4.1” condition share the same
underlying model; the only difference lies in the structured evidence block.

All outputs were independently evaluated by a clinical pharmacologist
(MD, PhD) with formal training in pharmacogenomics. The reviewer
applied a standardized 0–10 scoring rubric, where:
0–3 indicated incorrect or clinically misleading content,
4–6 represented partially aligned or incomplete recommendations,
7–8 reﬂected guideline-concordant outputs with minor omissions, and
9–10 denoted statements indistinguishable from reference CPIC
guidance.
The expert remained blinded to model identity throughout the
evaluation.
In addition to score-based evaluation, we performed a blinded, ran-
domized pairwise guideline-conformance assessment against CPIC refer-
ence recommendations. For each pharmacogenomic case, the expert
comparedanonymized pairs of modeloutputs and selected the option more
consistent with CPIC guidance, or indicated a tie or that neither option was
consistent. To minimize potential order and presentation bias, the order of
comparison cases and the left–right positioning of model outputs were
randomized. Pairwise outcomes were used to derive relative preference
rankings based on decisive comparisons. Pairwise win rates were computed
astheproportionofdecisivecomparisons(winsdividedbywinspluslosses),
with ties excluded from the denominator.
Full expert scoring results are available on Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/
zenodo.17727992)

Analysis and visualization
Quantitative evaluation results were analyzed using Python-based scientiﬁc
computing libraries. Pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank test was performed
using the scipy.stats module to assess differences in expert scores across
models. Data wrangling and metric computation were handled using
pandas and numpy. For visualization, we used matplotlib and seaborn.
